title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
hook: the power goes out on a night with no moon. the hymn's third verse begins in that kind of dark

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's second verse: no death, no deathlessness, no night or day, and That One, breathing without wind.

The power goes out on a night with no moon. You shut your eyes, then open them, and can't tell the difference. The dark behind your eyelids and the dark of the room have become one dark. Your hand is somewhere in front of your face, but you couldn't prove it. Nothing has an edge. The Nasadiya Sukta's third verse begins in that kind of dark, and pushes it further than any power cut could.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `EYES OPEN, EYES SHUT: THE SAME.` → `NOTHING HAS AN EDGE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit the verse opens tama asit tamasa gulham agre. Darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning. Not darkness covering something: darkness covering darkness. Nothing to see, and nothing to see it with. In paraphrase it goes on: all this was water, with no mark on it, nothing told apart from anything else. That's the hymn's picture of the start: not an empty space with sharp edges, but a sameness so complete that nothing could stand out. Then the turn. What was coming into being lay covered by emptiness, and that One was born by the power of tapas. Tapas is a word for heat. Later Hindu tradition also uses it for another heat, the glow a person builds through vows, fasting and long sitting. Here, at the very start, it's the warmth by which the One came to be. Notice what the verse leaves out. It doesn't say who made the heat, or name a god striking a spark. The hymn has asked questions it doesn't answer, and it keeps that honesty now. It only gives an order. First, sameness, dark on dark. Then warmth. Then one thing that could be told apart from the rest. A frozen pond is one flat gray sheet until warmth reaches it; then the ice gives, and the water starts to move. The hymn is talking about the beginning of everything, not ponds, but the shape is one a person can recognize: before anything has a name, something warms.
screen: `DARKNESS HIDDEN BY DARKNESS.` · `WATER WITH NO MARK ON IT.` · `THE ONE, BORN BY THE POWER OF HEAT.` · `SAMENESS, THEN WARMTH, THEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes or lower your gaze, and let the dark behind your eyelids be as plain as it is, without making pictures in it. Then find one warm place in the body, the breath at the nostrils, the hands resting together, the middle of the chest, and rest there, coming back whenever a thought pulls you off; if you pray, you can let that warmth be an offering.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its third verse, darkness hidden by darkness, until the One was born by the power of heat.
Your line: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation, who really knows? First dark on dark, then warmth. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: The Nasadiya Sukta is part of the Rig Veda, and like other Vedic hymns it is kept in traditional recitation, learned by memory from a teacher.

original.note: Sanskrit: heat. In Rig Veda 10.129.3 the One is born by its power; later texts also use it for the heat of discipline.

trapdoor: what you thought: a creation hymn starts with a maker doing something.
what it means: this verse starts with sameness, darkness hidden by darkness, and the One born by the power of heat.
what a scholar hears: tapasas tan mahinajayataikam, 'by the greatness of tapas that One was born,' with tapas the same word later used for the heat of ascetic discipline.

chat.says: What does that old creation hymn say got everything started?
options: Dark hidden by dark, it says, until the One was born by the power of heat.
Bright light first, it says, and then the dark was made out of it.
Cold, it says: everything began when a great fire went out.
chat.meaning: Rig Veda 10.129.3: darkness hidden by darkness, unmarked water, and the One born by the power of tapas, heat.

tapas.meaning: heat; later also the glow built by vows and discipline

notes: Days 1250 (verse 1) and 1251 (verse 2) were checked after writing; this day takes verse 3, and 1253–1255 take verses 4, 5 and 6–7. The review picks up 1251.
Sanskrit of 10.129.3a (tama āsīt tamasā gūḷham agre) and 3d (tapasas tan mahinājāyataikam) given from memory in simplified transliteration; confirm.
Paraphrase of 3b–c: 'all this was water with no mark on it' (apraketaṃ salilam), 'what was coming into being lay covered by emptiness' (tucchyenābhv apihitam). Confirm.
Claim that later Hindu texts use tapas for the heat of vows, fasting and austerity: standard, but confirm the wording. No etymology is claimed.
The kitchen and blank-page images are offered as the writer's analogy, explicitly not as the hymn's meaning.
